title: Extension to video and audio domains
description: The authors propose extending the DCGAN framework to other domains such as video (for frame prediction) and audio (pre-trained features for speech synthesis) as interesting future work.
canonical_description: framework not yet applied to non-image modalities like video and audio

evidence.anchor: extending this framework to other domains such as video
evidence.quote: We think that extending this framework to other domains such as video (for frame prediction) and audio (pre-trained features for speech synthesis) should be very interesting.

verdict.reasoning: Paper 2 (Emotional Speech DCGAN) directly extends the DCGAN framework to the audio modality via speech spectrograms, partially addressing the audio part of the gap. Paper 1 (MP3net) applies a convolutional GAN to raw audio but is not built on DCGAN and targets music, not speech synthesis. However, the video domain (frame prediction) is completely unaddressed by any paper, and even for audio the specific pre-trained-features-for-speech-synthesis task was not tackled. The gap thus remains meaningfully open in both scope and specificity.

paper.title: MP3net: coherent, minute-long music generation from raw audio with a simple convolutional GAN
paper.abstract: We present a deep convolutional GAN which leverages techniques from MP3/Vorbis audio compression to produce long, high-quality audio samples with long-range coherence. The model uses a Modified Discrete Cosine Transform (MDCT) data representation, which includes all phase information. Phase generation is hence integral part of the model. We leverage the auditory masking and psychoacoustic perception limit of the human ear to widen the true distribution and stabilize the training process. The model architecture is a deep 2D convolutional network, where each subsequent generator model block increases the resolution along the time axis and adds a higher octave along the frequency axis. The deeper layers are connected with all parts of the output and have the context of the full track. This enables generation of samples which exhibit long-range coherence. We use MP3net to create 95s stereo tracks with a 22kHz sample rate after training for 250h on a single Cloud TPUv2. An additional benefit of the CNN-based model architecture is that generation of new songs is almost instantaneous.

assessments.contribution_summary: MP3net presents a deep 2D convolutional GAN (inspired by ProGAN) that generates long, coherent raw audio samples using MDCT representation and psychoacoustic filtering. This demonstrates that convolutional GAN architectures can be successfully applied to the audio domain for raw waveform generation, addressing the audio part of the gap. The model produces 95-second stereo tracks with long-range coherence using a CNN-based architecture.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the video domain at all (frame prediction or otherwise). It also does not specifically extend the original DCGAN framework - instead it builds on more modern architectures like ProGAN, WGAN-GP, and self-attention mechanisms. The audio application is for music generation, not the specific audio tasks mentioned in the gap (pre-trained features for speech synthesis). Additionally, the paper does not frame itself as an extension of DCGAN specifically, but rather as a novel architecture inspired by ProGAN and audio compression techniques.
evidence_snippets: We present a deep convolutional GAN which leverages techniques from MP3/Vorbis audio compression to produce long, high-quality audio samples with long-range coherence.
The model architecture is a deep 2D convolutional network, where each subsequent generator model block increases the resolution along the time axis and adds a higher octave along the frequency axis.
The model architecture of MP3net is shown in figure [REF:fig:modelarchitecture]. The model is a WGAN with gradient penalty.

paper.title: Learning Representations of Emotional Speech with Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Automatically assessing emotional valence in human speech has historically been a difficult task for machine learning algorithms. The subtle changes in the voice of the speaker that are indicative of positive or negative emotional states are often "overshadowed" by voice characteristics relating to emotional intensity or emotional activation. In this work we explore a representation learning approach that automatically derives discriminative representations of emotional speech. In particular, we investigate two machine learning strategies to improve classifier performance: (1) utilization of unlabeled data using a deep convolutional generative adversarial network (DCGAN), and (2) multitask learning. Within our extensive experiments we leverage a multitask annotated emotional corpus as well as a large unlabeled meeting corpus (around 100 hours). Our speaker-independent classification experiments show that in particular the use of unlabeled data in our investigations improves performance of the classifiers and both fully supervised baseline approaches are outperformed considerably. We improve the classification of emotional valence on a discrete 5-point scale to 43.88% and on a 3-point scale to 49.80%, which is competitive to state-of-the-art performance.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper applies the DCGAN framework to the audio domain by using it to learn representations of emotional speech from spectrograms. The authors use a DCGAN with a multitask classifier (valence and activation) trained on both labeled emotional speech data (IEMOCAP) and unlabeled meeting speech data (AMI). They show that incorporating unlabeled data via the DCGAN's unsupervised learning improves emotional valence classification performance compared to fully supervised baselines. This constitutes an extension of DCGAN to the audio modality, specifically for speech emotion recognition.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper only partially addresses the gap. First, it applies DCGAN to audio but via spectrograms (2D image-like representations) rather than raw audio waveforms, so it does not demonstrate a true non-2D-modal extension. Second, the gap mentions video domain extension (frame prediction) which this paper does not address at all. Third, the gap specifically mentions "pre-trained features for speech synthesis" as the audio application, whereas this paper focuses on emotion recognition/classification, not speech synthesis. Finally, the paper does not explore whether the DCGAN approach generalizes to other audio tasks beyond emotional valence classification.
evidence_snippets: In this work we leverage RL strategies and automatically learn representations of emotional speech from the spectrogram directly using a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture.
we extend the CNN architecture to a deep convolutional generative neural network (DCGAN) that can be trained in an unsupervised fashion
Audio data is fed to the network models in the form of spectrograms.

paper.title: Adversarial Data Augmentation for Disordered Speech Recognition
paper.abstract: Automatic recognition of disordered speech remains a highly challenging task to date. The underlying neuro-motor conditions, often compounded with co-occurring physical disabilities, lead to the difficulty in collecting large quantities of impaired speech required for ASR system development. To this end, data augmentation techniques play a vital role in current disordered speech recognition systems. In contrast to existing data augmentation techniques only modifying the speaking rate or overall shape of spectral contour, fine-grained spectro-temporal differences between disordered and normal speech are modelled using deep convolutional generative adversarial networks (DCGAN) during data augmentation to modify normal speech spectra into those closer to disordered speech. Experiments conducted on the UASpeech corpus suggest the proposed adversarial data augmentation approach consistently outperformed the baseline augmentation methods using tempo or speed perturbation on a state-of-the-art hybrid DNN system. An overall word error rate (WER) reduction up to 3.05\% (9.7\% relative) was obtained over the baseline system using no data augmentation. The final learning hidden unit contribution (LHUC) speaker adapted system using the best adversarial augmentation approach gives an overall WER of 25.89% on the UASpeech test set of 16 dysarthric speakers.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper applies DCGANs to the audio domain for disordered speech data augmentation, where DCGANs are trained to transform normal speech spectrograms into those resembling dysarthric speech. The work focuses on improving ASR for disordered speech by generating augmented training data that captures fine-grained spectro-temporal characteristics of impaired speech. While it uses DCGANs on audio data (spectrograms), this is a specific application to disordered speech recognition, not a general extension of the DCGAN framework to audio or video domains as envisioned in the gap.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap specifically calls for extending the DCGAN framework to video (for frame prediction) and audio (pre-trained features for speech synthesis) as general-domain applications. This paper does not address video frame prediction at all. For audio, it uses DCGANs on spectrograms (2D image-like representations) for a specific data augmentation task in disordered speech recognition, rather than exploring DCGANs on raw audio waveforms or using pre-trained features for speech synthesis as the gap describes. The general question of how DCGANs can be adapted to non-image modalities (video, raw audio) remains entirely open.
evidence_snippets: In contrast to existing data augmentation techniques only modifying the speaking rate or overall shape of spectral contour, fine-grained spectro-temporal differences between disordered and normal speech are modelled using deep convolutional generative adversarial networks (DCGAN) during data augmentation to modify normal speech spectra into those closer to disordered speech.

The Generator component contains 4 convolutional layers, the first three of which have 8 kernels while the last one has 1 kernel only. All of the kernels in the Generator has a kernel size of 3 × 3 and stride of 1 × 1.
Future research will focus on improve GAN modelling on richer spectral and temporal characteristics of disordered speech.

paper.title: Facial Expression Video Generation Based-On Spatio-temporal Convolutional GAN: FEV-GAN
paper.abstract: Facial expression generation has always been an intriguing task for scientists and researchers all over the globe. In this context, we present our novel approach for generating videos of the six basic facial expressions. Starting from a single neutral facial image and a label indicating the desired facial expression, we aim to synthesize a video of the given identity performing the specified facial expression. Our approach, referred to as FEV-GAN (Facial Expression Video GAN), is based on Spatio-temporal Convolutional GANs, that are known to model both content and motion in the same network. Previous methods based on such a network have shown a good ability to generate coherent videos with smooth temporal evolution. However, they still suffer from low image quality and low identity preservation capability. In this work, we address this problem by using a generator composed of two image encoders. The first one is pre-trained for facial identity feature extraction and the second for spatial feature extraction. We have qualitatively and quantitatively evaluated our model on two international facial expression benchmark databases: MUG and Oulu-CASIA NIR&VIS. The experimental results analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach in generating videos of the six basic facial expressions while preserving the input identity. The analysis also proves that the use of both identity and spatial features enhances the decoder ability to better preserve the identity and generate high-quality videos. The code and the pre-trained model will soon be made publicly available.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper proposes FEV-GAN, a spatio-temporal convolutional GAN for generating facial expression videos from a single neutral face image and an expression label. It uses two encoders (identity and spatial) to improve video quality and identity preservation. The paper focuses on a specific application (facial expression video generation) using 3D convolutions, not on extending the DCGAN framework to video or audio domains.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the gap at all. The gap asks about extending the DCGAN framework (a specific architecture using transposed 2D convolutions) to video and audio domains. This paper: (1) does not use the DCGAN architecture — it uses 3D spatio-temporal convolutions with a dual-encoder design, which is a different framework; (2) does not frame its work as an extension of DCGAN; (3) does not address audio domain at all. The gap of extending DCGAN to video and audio remains completely open.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: Moderately tractable. Data is abundant (video datasets like UCF-101, speech datasets like LibriSpeech). Compute requirements are modest (DCGAN is a lightweight architecture by modern standards — video may need more memory but still fits a single GPU). Methodologically, the audio side has a partial solution (spectrogram-as-image approach from Paper 2), making it quite feasible to extend to the specific pre-trained-features-for-speech-synthesis goal. The video side is harder: frame prediction with a plain DCGAN requires architectural modifications (e.g., 3D convolutions or a temporal discriminator) and there are known failure modes (mode collapse, temporal inconsistency) that are not trivial to fix. However, prior work on video GANs provides a roadmap. Evaluation is clear (FVD, IS, MOS). Scope is two separate domains, which makes the gap somewhat broad, but each can be tackled independently. The main feasibility drag is that video frame prediction with a plain DCGAN is nontrivial — it's more than a simple layer swap.
